title: Level 3 - How to Salt Passwords for Improved Encryption
summary: Explains salting and bcrypt salt rounds as the defence against hash-table and brute-force attacks on hashed passwords, then upgrades the Express + Postgres secrets app to hash on register with bcrypt.hash and verify on login with bcrypt.compare.

concepts.heading: Why plain hashing is not enough
points: Human-chosen passwords are short and often dictionary words, so an attacker can precompute a table mapping common passwords to their hashes and simply look stored hashes up.
Identical passwords give identical hashes, which is how users sharing a password can be spotted in a leaked table.
Fast algorithms such as MD5 help the attacker: a GPU can compute billions of MD5 hashes per second, so even a salted MD5 table could be rebuilt quickly.

concepts.heading: What a salt is
points: A salt is a random string generated per user. It is combined with the password before hashing, so the hash is derived from both.
Because each user gets a different salt, two users with the same password end up with different hashes, and a precomputed table no longer works.
The user never sees or remembers the salt. It is stored in the database next to the hash.
To verify a login: take the typed password, combine it with that user's stored salt, hash it the same way and compare against the stored hash. The plain password is never stored.
(Extra) With the bcrypt library the salt is embedded inside the hash string itself (the $2b$10$... prefix holds the algorithm version, cost and salt), so there is no separate salt column to manage.

concepts.heading: Bcrypt: deliberately slow hashing
points: Bcrypt is an industry-standard password hashing algorithm built on the Blowfish cipher. Its value is that it is slow, so large-scale guessing becomes impractical.

Rough comparison given: top GPUs manage tens of billions of MD5 hashes per second but only around seventeen thousand bcrypt hashes per second. A salted table that takes seconds with MD5 would take months with bcrypt, so attackers move on to easier targets.
The npm package is called bcrypt; docs are on npm. It must be added to package.json dependencies and installed with npm install.

concepts.heading: Salt rounds (cost factor)
points: One round: hash(password + salt). Two rounds: feed the first hash plus the same salt through the hash function again. The number of repetitions is the salt rounds.
Each +1 on the setting roughly doubles the time to compute a hash. As hardware gets faster, raise the number (e.g. 10 now, 12 later) without changing algorithm or other code.
Pick a value balancing security against login/register latency. The course uses 10, which was fast enough on the machines tried. Too few rounds (e.g. 2) makes brute force much quicker.

concepts.heading: Registering: bcrypt.hash
points: Import with import bcrypt from "bcrypt" (project uses ES modules via "type": "module") and define const saltRounds = 10 near the top.
In the POST /register route, after the check that the email does not already exist and just before the INSERT, call bcrypt.hash(password, saltRounds, callback).
Arguments: the plain text to hash (req.body.password), the salt rounds, and a callback receiving (err, hash).
The existing INSERT and res.render("secrets.ejs") move inside the callback, because they must wait for the hash. Since the INSERT is awaited there, the callback is declared async.
Store hash in the password column instead of the plain password. On err, log it (at minimum console.log/console.error) and do not insert.

Test by registering a new user: the password column now holds a long unreadable string even though 123456 was typed. Delete earlier rows with plain-text passwords, since they no longer fit the scheme and can never log in.

concepts.heading: Logging in: bcrypt.compare
points: Hashing the login password again and comparing strings would not work, because salting makes each hash differ. Bcrypt provides compare for this.
Signature: bcrypt.compare(plainLoginPassword, storedHash, callback). Argument order matters: the plain text first, the stored hash second, so it knows which to hash and which to read the salt from.
The callback gets (err, result) where result is a boolean. true means match: render secrets.ejs. false: send an Incorrect Password message.
Rename variables for clarity: loginPassword for what the user typed in the form, storedHashedPassword for the database value.
The old plain equality check (if/else comparing strings) is deleted and replaced by the compare callback. The 'user not found' branch stays as before.
Test: correct password logs true and shows the secrets page; a wrong one such as qwerty shows the incorrect password message.

concepts.heading: Where this leaves the app
points: Even if the database leaks, only salted bcrypt hashes are exposed and there is no feasible way to recover the original passwords.
Next lesson adds cookies and sessions so a logged-in user does not have to sign in again on every visit.

task.name: Add bcrypt hashing and salting to the secrets app
task.starting_point: Project folder for this lesson (Authentication Lv.2 starter): index.js contains the previous lesson's working email/password app that still stores plain text passwords. package.json already lists bcrypt as a dependency. Postgres database named secrets with a users table (email, password) must be running.
task.goal: Passwords are hashed with bcrypt (10 salt rounds) on registration and verified with bcrypt.compare on login, so no plain text password is ever stored.
steps: Extract the lesson download, open it in VS Code, cd into the project and run npm install.
Import bcrypt and add const saltRounds = 10.
In POST /register, after the existing-user check, wrap the INSERT in bcrypt.hash(password, saltRounds, async (err, hash) => {...}); insert hash instead of the plain password; log any err.
Move res.render("secrets.ejs") into the same callback so it runs after the insert.
Run node index.js, register a new user and confirm in the database that the password column holds a long hash. Delete any old plain text user rows.
In POST /login, rename the form value to loginPassword and the database value to storedHashedPassword.
Replace the string equality if/else with bcrypt.compare(loginPassword, storedHashedPassword, callback); render secrets.ejs when result is true, otherwise send Incorrect Password.
Test a correct login and a wrong password.
task.expected_result: New users appear in the database with bcrypt hash strings; login works with the right password and shows an incorrect password message for a wrong one.

pitfalls: Swapping the argument order of bcrypt.compare (plain password first, stored hash second).
Comparing hash-of-login-password to the stored hash with ===; salting makes this always fail.
Leaving old plain text rows in the table; they cannot log in under the new scheme.
Forgetting async on the hash callback when it awaits db.query, or leaving res.render outside the callback so it runs before saving.
Raising saltRounds too high makes every register and login slow.
(Extra) The reference solution logs the generated hash to the console; avoid logging credentials-related values in real apps.
